clue.text: In the way of the old spirit on personal call? (With a lot of reserve, you might not want it.)

definitions.text: With a lot of reserve, you might not want it

parts.words: the old spirit on personal call
parts.note: a familiar is the spirit of old witchcraft that attends one person, at their call
a way of doing something is a manner

explanation.surface: A puzzling question about how ghosts behave on house calls, with an aside about shy people.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis is the definition: someone very reserved would rather you didn't treat them too chummily.
explanation.definitionFit: A chummy, over-intimate way of behaving is exactly what a very reserved person dislikes.

clue.text: One might be a good inside fighter.

definitions.text: One might be a good inside fighter.

parts.words: One might be a good inside fighter.
parts.note: a secret sympathiser who works for the enemy from within; 'inside fighter' sounds like boxing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside fighter' is boxing language for a close-range puncher, but here it is someone fighting from inside a country for its enemy.
explanation.definitionFit: The term comes from the Spanish Civil War: a covert group of supporters within a city aiding the four columns attacking it.

clue.text: A haven for the 14, in extreme cases.

definitions.text: A haven for the 14, in extreme cases.

parts.words: A haven for the 14, in extreme cases.
parts.note: 14 is the answer to 14-across, the anxious and disturbed; in the worst cases they were once sent to this institution

explanation.walkthrough: The 14 refers to the answer to 14-across, NEUROTIC. 'Haven' is fair, since asylum first meant a place of refuge.
explanation.definitionFit: The old name for a hospital for the mentally ill pairs the word for refuge with a word for the mind.

clue.text: Slangy equivalent for mitts.

definitions.text: Slangy equivalent for mitts.

parts.note: mitts is slang for hands, and this American slang phrase for hands means the same

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mitts' looks like gloves, but it is already slang for hands; the answer is another slang word for them, the hooks you eat lunch with.
explanation.definitionFit: Old American slang calls the hands by the image of hooks used to grab food at a meal.

clue.text: Straightens out a sling shot.

definitions.text: Straightens out

indicators.note: shot in the sense of ruined or broken, so the letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone straightens a catapult so it fires true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sling shot' reads as one thing, a catapult, but 'shot' is the signal that rearranges ASLING.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring things into a straight line or correct position is to put them in line.

clue.text: What does the poor French sailor have to complain about?

definitions.text: What does the poor French sailor have to complain about?

parts.words: What does the poor French sailor have to complain about?
parts.note: the French phrase for seasickness is literally 'illness of the sea', mal meaning bad or poorly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' reads as pity for the sailor, but it hints at French mal, bad; the complaint is a medical one.
explanation.definitionFit: Seasickness, the sailor's ailment, is called in French by a phrase meaning sickness of the sea.

clue.text: You might file the digital type with "L," in a bunch of letters.

definitions.text: You might file the digital type

indicators.note: the letters are bunched together in a heap and come out in a new order

parts.note: the letter L, quoted in the clue

explanation.surface: Office filing instructions: put the fingernail sort in with the L folder, among a batch of correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bunch of letters' sounds like a pile of post, but it tells you to jumble the letters of L with IN A; 'digital' means of the fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: A fingernail grows on a digit, and people smooth it down with a nail file.

clue.text: Objective, for me? It's one possibility.

definitions.text: Objective, for me? It's one possibility.

parts.words: Objective, for me? It's one possibility.
parts.note: me is the objective case of I; that case is one possibility, as the grammatical case varies

explanation.walkthrough: 'Objective' looks like a goal, but it is the grammatical case: 'me' is in the objective case, and the stock phrase hedging between possibilities also names a case.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means according to whichever circumstances apply, and 'case' doubles here as a grammatical term.

clue.text: More commonly, being given a little bread?

definitions.text: More commonly, being given a little bread?

parts.words: More commonly, being given a little bread?
parts.note: bread is slang for money; the everyday, more common phrase for being handed some money is the answer

explanation.walkthrough: Bread here is the slang sense, money, not the loaf; 'More commonly' asks for the ordinary phrase for that slangy idea.
explanation.definitionFit: Grants or handouts of money to someone in need are described in standard English by this phrase.

clue.text: One used to stick his arm out all the way for it!

definitions.text: One used to stick his arm out all the way for it!

parts.words: One used to stick his arm out all the way for it!
parts.note: before indicator lights, a driver on the right-hand side of the road signalled this manoeuvre by holding the arm straight out of the window

explanation.walkthrough: In the old American hand signals, the arm held straight out meant turning left; bent upward or downward meant right or stopping.
explanation.definitionFit: The fully extended arm was the standard driver's hand signal for turning towards the left.

clue.text: Not the Master of the Foxhounds — his trophy may be subsequently reduced.

definitions.text: Not the Master of the Foxhounds — his trophy may be subsequently reduced.

parts.words: Not the Master of the Foxhounds — his trophy may be subsequently reduced.
parts.note: this hunter's trophy is a human head, which some cultures shrank afterwards, unlike the fox's brush taken by a Master of Foxhounds

explanation.walkthrough: The Master of Foxhounds leads an English fox hunt and keeps the fox's tail as a trophy; this other hunter's trophy is a shrunken head.
explanation.definitionFit: Some tribal warriors took enemies' heads as trophies and shrank them, which is what this hunter's name describes.

clue.text: The first person to take quiet command, as a net result.

definitions.text: net result

parts.note: me is the first-person pronoun in its object form
sh is the command telling someone to be quiet

explanation.surface: Someone takes charge and silences the room, and the outcome is described as a net gain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Net result' sounds like accounting, but it means the result of netting: the fabric of a net.
explanation.definitionFit: Mesh is the open, criss-crossed fabric that a net is made of.

clue.text: Broken dates — press not invited if you have this.

definitions.text: not invited if you have this

indicators.note: the words are broken up and their letters reassembled

explanation.surface: Missed appointments, and the reporters are kept out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' tells you to rearrange the letters of DATES and PRESS. The definition is a sentence frame: if you have done this, you went where you were not invited.
explanation.definitionFit: Entering someone's land or property without permission is the offence, so having done it means you came uninvited.

clue.text: One on a rostrum, alternatively on a mountain.

definitions.text: One on a rostrum

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
a tor is a rocky hill, especially on Dartmoor in south-west England

explanation.surface: A speaker who might stand on a platform, or else on a mountain top.
explanation.definitionFit: A rostrum is a raised platform for public speakers, and the person standing on it addresses the audience.

clue.text: Disturbed by the conflict, with no cure, it might seem.

definitions.text: Disturbed

indicators.note: the letters are in conflict, fighting one another into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone troubled by a war, beyond any remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbed by the conflict' reads as one phrase, but 'Disturbed' alone is the definition and 'conflict' stirs NOCUREIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone mentally disturbed and over-anxious is described by this word from psychology.

clue.text: Semicircular canals might be found there.

definitions.text: Semicircular canals might be found there.

parts.words: Semicircular canals might be found there.
parts.note: the three semicircular canals that control balance are in the deepest part of the ear

explanation.walkthrough: 'Canals' suggests waterways, but these are the fluid-filled loops in the head that sense balance.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatomy places the balance-sensing loops, beside the cochlea, in the innermost section of the hearing organ.

clue.text: Taking your drawers off a wooden frame? Quite the opposite!

definitions.text: Taking your drawers off a wooden frame? Quite the opposite!

parts.words: Taking your drawers off a wooden frame? Quite the opposite!
parts.note: drawers here are oxen that draw a plough or cart; the wooden frame is the yoke, taken off them rather than they off it

explanation.walkthrough: Drawers suggests underwear or a chest of drawers, but here it means animals that draw a load. You take the wooden yoke off the oxen, which is 'the opposite' of taking them off it.
explanation.definitionFit: Freeing draught oxen by removing the wooden crossbar fixed over their necks is this act.

clue.text: Puts to the test, just as the fool is about to speak?

definitions.text: Puts to the test

indicators.note: the fool is about to speak, so this phrase is heard rather than read

parts.note: a fool is an ass, and 'the fool is about to speak' gives ASS SAYS

explanation.surface: Testing someone at the very moment the jester opens his mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The fool' is ASS and his speaking SAYS; 'about to speak' says to hear the phrase aloud, and 'ass says' spoken runs into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To assay a metal or ore is to test its purity, so the word means puts something to a trial.

clue.text: Such tales as Frankenstein might be obtained by the sound associated with an abundance of spirit.

definitions.text: Such tales as Frankenstein

parts.note: got means obtained

parts.words: the sound associated with an abundance of spirit
parts.note: hic is the hiccup of someone who has drunk too much spirit

explanation.surface: Horror stories like Frankenstein seem to be conjured up by the noise of a haunting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' suggests ghosts in a horror tale, but it is alcohol, and the sound is a drunk's hiccup.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Shelley's novel is a classic of the genre of gloomy, supernatural horror fiction named after medieval architecture.

clue.text: Your name is probably a proper one.

definitions.text: Your name is probably a proper one.

parts.words: Your name is probably a proper one.
parts.note: a personal name is, in grammar

explanation.walkthrough: 'Proper' sounds like praise of your name, but it is the grammar term: names of particular people are proper nouns.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar, names of particular people and places belong to the word class called proper nouns.

clue.text: Literally, it's a thing to be remembered.

definitions.text: Literally, it's a thing to be remembered.

parts.words: Literally, it's a thing to be remembered.
parts.note: the Latin word translates word for word as 'a thing to be remembered'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Literally' points to the Latin original: the word is a gerundive of memorare, to remember.
explanation.definitionFit: A note written to remind oneself or others takes its name from the Latin for something that must be remembered.

clue.text: Your pipe isn't quite full, so how about a little cheese?

definitions.text: a little cheese

indicators.note: not quite the full word: its last letter is missing

parts.note: a brier (or briar) is a tobacco pipe carved from briar root

explanation.surface: A smoker's pipe is half-empty, so they are offered some cheese instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Brie is a soft French cheese, and the clue offers a small piece of it.

clue.text: It's not intended just to hold up your pants, though it might help in an emergency.

definitions.text: It's not intended just to hold up your pants, though it might help in an emergency.

parts.words: It's not intended just to hold up your pants, though it might help in an emergency.
parts.note: the rescue device is a lifebuoy fitted with a pair of canvas trousers, which the rescued person sits in

explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like a belt or braces; the device is a ring buoy with canvas trousers attached, hauled along a rope to bring people ashore from a wreck.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea rescues from stranded ships used a lifebuoy with built-in trousers slung from a rope, named for the old word for trousers.

clue.text: Keep decent care of it, but you'll have to come first.

definitions.text: come first

indicators.note: make something of it: the words before are to be reworked into something else

explanation.surface: Advice to look after something properly, though you must put yourself first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of it' asks you to make something of the words before: the fourteen letters of 'Keep decent care' rearrange into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To have priority over others, ranking or going ahead of them, is the meaning of this idiom.
